title: Who’s Afraid of Chinese Surpluses?
gist: China posted the largest trade surplus in history last year with exports still growing, and Project Syndicate contributors are split three ways on the right response: protectionism to force rebalancing, skepticism that tariffs help at all, or the view that fears of a new 'China shock' are overblown because the surpluses do more good than harm.

themes.theme: Record Chinese trade surplus and the policy debate

insights.claim: China recorded the largest trade surplus in its history last year, and its exports continue to grow.
insights.speaker: PS EDITORS
insights.so_what: A record and still-rising Chinese trade surplus is a headline macro data point that underpins ongoing tariff and rebalancing debates in the US and EU.
insights.quote: China recorded the largest trade surplus in history last year, and its exports continue to grow.

insights.claim: There is considerable disagreement among economists over both the scale of the threat China's trade surpluses pose to the global economy and the appropriate policy response.
insights.speaker: PS EDITORS
insights.so_what: Signals no policy consensus exists yet, meaning trade-policy outcomes toward China remain genuinely uncertain and worth tracking across multiple analyst camps rather than assuming one dominant view.
insights.quote: the scale of the threat to the global economy, and the appropriate response, remains subject to considerable disagreement

insights.claim: One camp of economists advocates protectionist measures against China, arguing tariffs are needed if only to pressure Beijing into committing to economic rebalancing.
insights.speaker: PS EDITORS
insights.so_what: Represents the pro-tariff camp's rationale (leverage for rebalancing, not just protection) — useful framing for gauging the political logic behind Western tariff proposals.
insights.quote: Some economists advocate protectionist measures, if only to pressure China to commit to economic rebalancing
insights.locator: paragraph beginning “China recorded the largest trade surplus”

insights.claim: A second camp of economists argues that tariffs on Chinese goods won't actually help address the underlying imbalance.
insights.speaker: PS EDITORS
insights.so_what: Highlights a credible skeptical view that tariff-based responses to Chinese surpluses may be ineffective, a risk factor for anyone positioned on the assumption tariffs will meaningfully shrink the trade gap.
insights.quote: others argue that tariffs won’t help
insights.locator: paragraph beginning “China recorded the largest trade surplus”

insights.claim: A third camp views the fear of a new 'China shock' as a bogeyman, arguing that China's surpluses actually do more good than harm to the global economy.
insights.speaker: PS EDITORS
insights.so_what: A genuinely against-consensus framing that Chinese export surpluses could be net-beneficial globally (e.g., cheaper goods, disinflationary pressure) — worth weighing against the more dominant protectionist narrative.
insights.quote: still others think the specter of another “China shock” is a bogeyman, because China’s surpluses do more good than harm
insights.locator: paragraph beginning “China recorded the largest trade surplus”

insights.claim: The roundup on Chinese surpluses features perspectives from PS editors and contributors Michael R. Strain, Desmond Lachman, Daniel Gros, Gene Frieda, Jeffrey Frankel, and Dani Rodrik.
insights.speaker: PS EDITORS
insights.so_what: Identifies the named economists whose fuller individual arguments (in linked companion pieces) are worth following for more granular positioning views on China trade policy.
